case_name: Northam Distributor Ltd. v Roman Hardware Inc.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Northam Distributor Ltd. v. Roman
Hardware Inc.,

2024 BCSC 2594

Date: 20241107

Docket:
S249622

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Northam Distributor Ltd. and 1057079 B.C. Ltd.

Plaintiffs

And:

Roman Hardware Inc.,
Dilpreet Singh Joura and Jasbir Singh Kochar

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Sharma

Oral Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Counsel for the Plaintiffs:

H. Hehar

Counsel for the Defendant Roman Hardware
Inc.:

M.K.
Shergill

Place and Date of Hearing:

New
Westminster, B.C.

November
5, 2024

Place and Date of Judgment:

New
Westminster, B.C.

November
7, 2024

This is the written version of judgment
rendered orally on November 7, 2024. It has been edited to correct or improve
grammar and style, and add case citations, but no other changes have been made.

[
1
]

THE COURT:
The
defendant Roman Hardware Inc. (“Roman”) seeks an order under R. 9‑5(1)
of
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, striking out the claims made in the
amended notice of civil claim (“ANOCC”) against it.

[
2
]

In the alternative, it seeks an order pursuant
to R. 9‑6 summarily dismissing the proceeding against it. In the
further alternative, it seeks security for costs within 14 days in the amount
of $31,133, the estimated costs for a 10‑day trial. It also seeks costs.

[
3
]

The plaintiffs, Northam Distributer Ltd.
(“Northam”) and 1057079 BC Ltd. (“105”), oppose all relief sought. The
defendants Dilpreet Joura and Jasbir Kochar (“Personal Defendants”) did not
appear on this application.

[
4
]

This dispute is about a non‑compete clause
that the Personal Defendants entered into with the plaintiffs. It is not
disputed that in March 2021, the plaintiff 105 purchased shares in Northam from
Wipro, a company owned by the Personal Defendants, for about $1.2 million.
The content of that agreement, as well as the validity and content of what
constitutes the non‑compete clause, are in dispute amongst the parties.

[
5
]

The notice of civil claim was filed June 21,
2023, and then amended shortly thereafter on June 30, 2023. A response was
filed by all defendants in August 2023, and a counterclaim was filed by the
Personal Defendants. The plaintiffs filed a response to the counterclaim in
November 2023.

[
6
]

In the original notice of civil claim, the
plaintiffs did not plead a cause of action against Roman, but made an
allegation about its failing to disclose certain documents. Not long after that
and shortly before the claim was amended, Roman disclosed those documents — the
Central Securities Register and Register of Directors.

[
7
]

In April 2024, the plaintiffs filed a motion
seeking an interlocutory injunction against the Personal Defendants. That was
heard last month and remains under reserve.

[
8
]

During the agreement to purchase shares, the Personal
Defendants entered into a restrictive covenant that would not allow them, for a
period of five years, to compete with the plaintiffs in BC, Alberta, and
Saskatchewan in the kitchen cabinet and shower door hardware business. The
defendant Roman is engaged in the business of selling cabinet hardware and
other similar products.

[
9
]

The plaintiffs allege that Roman sells these
products out of a shop located in Surrey run by Onex Enterprises Inc. (“Onex”),
which is owned by one of the Personal Defendants. The registered owner of the
shop at that address is Wipro, again, owned by one of the Personal Defendants.
The plaintiffs allege that the Personal Defendants are, in fact, involved in
the day‑to‑day operations in Roman and thereby are breaching the
non‑compete clause.

[
10
]

The test for striking a claim under R. 9‑5(1)(a) is that
it must be plain and obvious, assuming the facts as pleaded are true, that the
claim discloses no cause of action or reasonable prospect of success:
Watchel
v. British Columbia
,
2019 BCSC 1087
;
Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,

2020 SCC 5
. These cases indicate the threshold to strike a claim as not
demonstrating a cause of action is high.

[
11
]

Roman contends that the allegations against it, even as set out in
the
ANOCC
, are deficient as being, among other
things, unspecified, vague, and lacking full particulars with respect to the claim
of civil conspiracy. Specifically, Roman submits that the pleading fails to
identify material facts supporting the allegation that Roman became aware of
the non‑compete clause, or that someone was breaching it. As I noted,
this is a test applied to the pleadings alone, and Roman says that the
pleadings on their face are insufficient.

[
12
]

Specifically, Roman points to the claims made in
the ANOCC under the heading “"Civil Conspiracy”, which I reproduce here:

U.   Two or more of the defendants named in this proceeding acted in
concert, by agreement, or in the alternative, with a common design or
intention.

V.    The co-conspirators engaged in conduct which breached the SPA.

W.   The conduct was directed towards the plaintiffs.

X.    At all material times, the co-conspirators knew, or ought to
have known, that injury was likely to result.

Y.    The plaintiffs
suffered damages as a direct result of the defendants’ conspiracy.

[
13
]

Roman points out that, at paragraph U, it simply states that “two or
more of the defendants … acted in concert”, and that on its own, the allegation
is vague because it does not identify exactly who was acting in concert. Roman complains
that the allegation at paragraph V of a co-conspirator engaging in conduct that
breached the agreement, is without definition or identification of, among other
things, the impugned conduct, how Roman was involved, or how Roman knew about
it.

[
14
]

Roman relies on
Equustek Solutions Inc. v.
Jack
,
2024 BCCA 104
as an example of how pleading for conspiracy should be
set out with regard to the identification of material facts (which it says is
missing in the matter at hand):

[126]    The judge set out the portions of
the appellants’ pleading related to the alleged conspiracy:

[338]    The conspiracy in this case is
delineated in the pleadings in the following terms:

33. At a time unknown to the Plaintiffs,
the Defendants Jack, Colin Marsh, Kathleen Marsh, Crawford, Ingraham, Bunker,
Igor Cheifot, Alexander Cheifot, Geiger, Alfonso Doe, and John Doe, and those
of the Datalink Companies that were then in existence,
agreed to act in
concert using unlawful means to destroy Equustek’s business in order that they
could appropriate all of Equustek’s business, profits, and goodwill for
themselves.

34. This intention to harm the Plaintiffs
was the predominant purpose of the Defendants at all material times.

35. The acts done in furtherance of the
conspiracy, and the unlawful means used, include:

a.
Stealing the Plaintiffs’ Trade
Secrets
, below, in order to build the Datalink Products, as set out below;

b.
Claiming Equustek’s products as their
own
, and misrepresenting to the public that their own products were an
upgrade or replacement of the Equustek products, which they said were no longer
available;

c.
Using the Plaintiffs’ trademarks to
drive traffic to the Datalink websites
on the false pretense that they
intended to sell the Equustek products under the Distribution Agreement;

d.
Breaching the Distribution Agreement
;

e.
Infringing the Plaintiff’s copyrights
;

f. Organizing their assets and their
corporate structure to make it as difficult as possible for the plaintiffs to
identify who is involved,
recover their intellectual property
, or
collect any damages;

g. Using false names in their
dealings
with their customers
;

h. Using false names in their
communications with one another, in order to create a false documentary record
to be revealed in this litigation, in order to make it as difficult as possible
for the plaintiffs to discover the truth about these events;

i. Giving false or misleading evidence and
further concealing documents in these proceedings, in order to prevent the
plaintiffs from discovering the full scale of the conspiracy;

j. Continuing to carry on business, or
assisting Jack and the Datalink Companies to carry on business, after they had
been prohibited from doing so by orders of this court;

k. Carrying on their scheme under multiple
fictional corporate names … [names listed]

And further particulars are set out in the
balance of this Statement of Facts.

[Emphasis in original.]

[
15
]

In response, the plaintiffs say that pleadings
should not be measured on a standard of perfection, and in any event, their
pleading is sufficient. They point to other portions of the ANOCC that they say
provide sufficient detail to pass this test, including:

F.    In 2022, it came to the attention of Northam and 1057079 that
Joura and Kochar had been competing with Northam and 1057079 in a manner which
was in breach of the SPA, by becoming involved in the running of business for
Roman.

G.   At all material times, Joura’s and Kochar’s involvement in
Roman’s business was deliberate, calculated and strategically carried out, the
details of which are better known to the defendants.

H.   At all material times, Roman was aware of and aided in Joura’s and
Kochar’s breach of the non-competition clause contained in the SPA, for
business gains and did in fact secure business gains, the particulars of which
are better known to the defendants.

I.     At all material
times, Joura and Kochar intended on profiting from making contributions to
Roman, and did obtain such profit(s), the details of which are better known to
the defendants.

[
16
]

In summary, the plaintiffs argue that Roman’s conduct constituting a
conspiracy was allowing the Personal Defendants to get involved in Roman’s
business for the purpose of competing against the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs allege
Roman was aware of the non-compete and allowing the Personal Defendants to
become involved in its business, Roman abetted in a breach of the agreement for
the purpose of making profits.

[
17
]

The plaintiffs rely on
Garcha Bros Meat Shop
Ltd. v. Singh
,
2022 BCCA 36
[
Garcha Bros
], which dealt with a dispute
amongst a franchisee and principals. They specifically rely on the following
passage:

[36]      There is no doubt that the
franchisor pleaded conspiracy in para 32 of its + notice of civil claim:

Kuldip [Singh], Kulwinder [Sandhu], and
Arshpreet [Singh] conspired to incorporate [1127] for the purpose of defeating
the non‑competition obligations of the Franchisee.

[
18
]

The plaintiffs say that if the above wording was considered
sufficient, their pleadings are sufficient and meet the test.

[
19
]

However, Roman points out that the pleading in
Garcha Bros
is
superior because it actually identified the particular defendants alleged to
have conspired, as well as the particular conduct that amount to a conspiracy (incorporating
a company).

[
20
]

Roman emphasizes the following comments from
Owimar
v. Stewart
,
2019 BCSC 1198
:

[19]      Rather than plead material facts,
the Claim contains numerous speculative propositions and bald statements of
wrongdoing in relation to the plaintiff’s medical testing and against ICBC and
its counsel, Mr. Stewart, in relation to the plaintiff’s motor vehicle actions.
Care must be taken to avoid undermining the role of pleadings in identifying
the issues by allowing a party to plead bald assertions or mere conclusory
statements of law. A bald assertion of a conclusion is not a pleading of
material fact:

[18]      There is no bright line between
material facts and bald allegations, nor between pleadings of material facts
and the prohibition on pleading of evidence. They are points on a continuum,
and it is the responsibility of a motions judge, looking at the pleadings as a
whole, to ensure that the pleadings define the issues with sufficient precision
to make the pre‑trial and trial proceedings both manageable and fair.

[19]      What constitutes a material fact
is determined in light of the cause of action and the damages sought to be
recovered. The plaintiff must plead, in summary form but with sufficient
detail, the constituent elements of each cause of action or legal ground
raised. The pleading must tell the defendant who, when, where, how and what
gave rise to its liability.

Mancuso v. Canada (Minister of National
Health and Welfare)
,
2015 FCA 227
at paras.
18‑19
& 27
.

[20]      However,
even assuming the facts in the Claim to be true, the plaintiff still has no chance
of succeeding and the Claim is sure to fail due the numerous radical defects in
it:
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R.
263 at para.
15
. The requirement to assume the facts pleaded to be true does
not prevent skeptical analysis in the case of purely speculative allegations or
assumptions:
Green v. Proline Management Limited
,
2017 BCSC 1656
at
para.
35
. Speculative and fanciful claims in a pleading may also demonstrate
that it is plain and obvious no cause of action is disclosed:
Olenga v.
British Columbia
,
2015 BCSC 1050
at paras.
17 and 21
.

[
21
]

Roman emphasizes that while perfection is not
needed, there must be something more than a bald assertion. Simply making a
conclusory statement does not satisfy the requirement to plead a material fact.
Roman submits that the proposition from
Owimar
that “[t]he requirement
to assume the facts pleaded to be true does not prevent skeptical analysis in
the case of purely speculative allegations or assumptions” applies here: at
para. 20.

[
22
]

Roman also submits that that the plaintiffs’ reliance on paragraphs F
to I of the ANOCC does not assist because those paragraphs are not under the
portion of the claim identified as constituting the facts for conspiracy.
Instead, they are under the heading for breach of a non‑competition
agreement. Accordingly, Roman submits that does not alleviate the problems they
have identified with the plaintiffs’ claim.

[
23
]

Moreover, Roman points to another deficiency in the pleadings: Roman
is not a party to the share purchase agreement, and therefore, cannot be said
to be bound by the non‑compete clause.

[
24
]

However, in
Garcha Bros
,
a similar argument was made, but the
court granted an injunction restraining not only the franchisee and its principals,
but the appellants, who were not privy to the franchise agreement: at para. 2.
That accords with my understanding of the law, which is that a claim for breach
of a competition agreement could not be sustained individually against Roman—it
might be sustained through the route of the plea of conspiracy.

[
25
]

With regard to that point, I agree with the plaintiffs that one must
read the ANOCC as a whole. While it may have been preferable to articulate the alleged
facts that constitute conspiracy under the proper heading, I find one must read
all claims together. On that standard, while the plea is not very detailed, the
claim of conspiracy is supported by allegations of material facts.

[
26
]

When making a claim for predominant purpose conspiracy, a plaintiff's
obligation is to establish three things: (i) an agreement or concerted action
between two or many persons; (ii) with the predominant purpose of causing
injury; and (iii) that overt acts committed cause damage to the plaintiff. The plaintiffs
in this case say that the act in question is Roman’s allowing the Personal Defendants
to be involved in its business, which constitutes the “agreement” that ended up
creating a conspiracy.

The Application to Strike Pleadings

[
27
]

Striking a claim under R. 9‑5(1)(d) — that it is “plain
and obvious” a claim cannot succeed — has a high threshold. It is meant to dismiss
claims that have no chance of success as they are pleaded.

[
28
]

I do not find that Roman has met that test in this case. While the
pleading against Roman is not detailed, I am unable to conclude it has no
chance of success. Looking at the claim as a whole, there is sufficient
assertion of material facts that may constitute conspiracy.

[
29
]

Roman also relies on the other subsections in R. 9‑5(1),
mainly those in (b), (c), and (d). Counsel appropriately addressed each
subsection separately, but I find it more convenient to address them together
because of the commonalities in the legal test, which I will comment on first.

[
30
]

Under R. 9‑5(1)(b)–(c), pleadings that are said to be
embarrassing, frivolous or vexation or unnecessary can lead to the court
striking them. “Embarrassing” in that sense refers to failing to state the real
issue in an intelligible way. That test has some commonality with abuse of
process in R. 9‑5(1)(d).

[
31
]

Under R. 9‑5(1)(b), "scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious" typically means the pleadings lacks a
bona fide

legal argument and is, in fact, intended to harass or embarrass, and therefore,
serves no legitimate purpose:
Young v. Borzoni et al
,
2007 BCCA 16
. That
particular formulation of the test also has some commonality to abuse of
process.

[
32
]

A helpful discussion is in
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2013 BCSC 1143
,
where Justice Voith discusses the basic test for each subsection illustrating how
abuse of process is, in some ways, the underlying foundation to or can be seen
as an umbrella for all of the other subsections.

[58]      In this case, having regard to the
numerous and varied deficiencies in the Proposed Pleading, I am satisfied that
it should not be filed. There was some suggestion by some of the Defendants
that I ought not to allow the Plaintiffs to redraft the Proposed Pleading. In
The
Owners, Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holdings Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 473
at
paras.
40‑43
, Justice Sinclair Prowse described both the authorities that
addressed the circumstances in which a party will not be permitted to redraft
pleadings that were struck by the court as well as the conceptual basis for the
exercise of that discretion.

[59]      The notices of application that
were filed by the Defendants do not seek any such relief nor do I consider that
it would be appropriate, for various reasons, to limit the Plaintiffs’ ability
to amend and file a proper claim.

[60]      The courts will, to the extent
reasonably possible and depending on the history of a matter, extend some
indulgence to a self‑represented litigant who is not conversant with the Rules
or the law. Such indulgences do not, however, extend to any diminution or
impairment of another party's substantive rights. Allowing the Proposed
Pleading to be filed, for example, would impair the ability of the Defendants
to respond to and defend the claims being made against them. It would render
their defence inefficient. It would impede their intended application to strike
all or parts of the claims being made against them. An indulgence granted to a
self‑represented litigant cannot extend this far.

[61]      Providing the Plaintiffs a further
opportunity to prepare a proper claim does not engage these concerns. Having
said this, other concerns do arise. In
Broadfoot 2011
and
Broadfoot
2008
, Justices Silverman and Williams, respectively, identified various
deficiencies in the pleadings advanced by Dr. and Mrs. Sahyoun. Some of those
deficiencies are repeated in the Proposed Pleading. Furthermore, in
Broadfoot
2008
, Justice Williams addressed Dr. and Mrs. Sahyoun’s attacks on various
administrative decision‑makers and observed:

[80]      I reach my conclusion having
carefully examined the statement of claim. While it is important to be cautious
of allegations that they are really just attacks on the decision dressed up to
allege serious bad faith misconduct, the court must bear carefully in mind the
test which is to be employed in assessing this application and to which I
adverted earlier. It must be assumed that the facts alleged can be proved.

[62]      These comments resonate in the
present case. The Proposed Pleading contains numerous serious allegations of
fraudulent misrepresentation, falsification of materials, perjury and malicious
behavior on the part of numerous unrelated defendants. It is open to a
plaintiff, on a proper basis, to advance some of these matters either
independently or in support of an action if a proper foundation exists for the
allegation. It is thoroughly wrong to do so for strategic reasons. I have
explained to Dr. and Mrs. Sahyoun that they must reflect carefully on what
allegations they advance and should be mindful of the sanctions that
potentially exist where a claim of this nature is not made out.

[63]      I am
ordering the Plaintiffs to provide the Defendants with a further amended notice
of civil claim, which complies with Rule 3‑1, within 60 days of receipt
of these reasons. That timeframe provides the Plaintiffs ample time to reflect
on these reasons and to make the amendments that are required. It also
recognizes that the Defendants have been seeking to obtain a proper pleading
from the Plaintiffs for many months and that they wish to address the claims
being made against them.

[
33
]

Roman submits that even if one looks at the whole ANOCC incorporating
the facts asserted in paragraphs F to I under the conspiracy claim, there is a
lack of particularity. Roman contends that it is not an intelligible pleading to
which it can respond. It submits the pleading of a conspiracy lacks precise
detail as to what the agreement was, how it was formed, how Roman became aware
of it, and what it was meant to do.

[
34
]

In particular, Roman points to what it says is the vague pleading
made in paragraph I that somehow, the Personal Defendants made contributions to
Roman for profit. Roman alleges that it is entirely unclear what that is
supposed to mean.

[
35
]

With regard to abuse of process, Roman points out that in the
original notice of civil claim, it was not named as a party and was only listed
in terms of failing to disclose certain documents. It was only after getting those
document that the plaintiffs then amended the claim, or at least, around the
same time. Roman asserts that this may have been a strategic sequence of
pleadings, in that it was a way to get access to documents that normally, the
plaintiffs would not have. Roman submits being named in the original notice of
civil claim was for a collateral purpose of getting access to the documents in
order to get a “leg up” in the litigation.

[
36
]

Although I find that Roman's points about the lack of particularity
in the civil claim has a sound basis, overall, I am not satisfied that satisfies
any of the tests, especially for abuse of process, as set out in R. 9‑5(1)(b),
(c), or (d).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    In
a way, Roman relies on the same grounds it raised under R. 9‑5(1)(a),
albeit now pointing to some evidence. I am not being critical of counsel: it
was appropriate to argue that the same factors could substantiate meeting the
test under the other subsections. However, I am not persuaded that these
pleadings are embarrassing or speculative in the sense that the case law talks
about.

[
37
]

The claim of conspiracy is tied to the alleged breach of the non‑compete
clause, and, therefore, it is tied to those allegations of facts, even if those
might be characterized as a bit thin. That allegation is Roman’s permitting the
Personal Defendants, who were bound by the non‑compete agreement, to get
involved in Roman’s operations amounted to a breach of the non‑compete,
which is the underpinnings of a claim of conspiracy.

[
38
]

For all those reasons, I am not satisfied that Roman has met the
test to strike the pleading under Rule 9‑5(1).

Summary Dismissal

[
39
]

Roman also applies, in the alternative, for summary dismissal of the
claim under R. 9‑6 and appropriately refers to the leading case from
the Supreme Court of Canada,
Canada (Attorney General) v. Lameman
,
2008
SCC 14
[
Lameman
]. Several basic principles about summary judgment were
set out in that case. Among these is that the rule serves the important purpose
of preventing claims or defences that have no chance of success from proceeding
to trial. The test to meet again is high, but it is not restricted to the
pleadings:
Lameman
at paras.
10–11
.

[
40
]

The idea is that if the court is satisfied there is no genuine issue
for trial, it should pronounce judgment in favour of the defendant. The onus is
on the party applying for summary trial to show that there is no triable issue,
and that the other party is bound to lose. It is acknowledged that this is a
very high standard:
Rahman v. Windermere Valley Property Management Ltd.
,

2021 BCSC 118
.

[
41
]

The case law confirms that the test of “no genuine issue existing” can
be made out when it is manifestly clear, or beyond doubt, that the party is
bound to lose. The policy underlying this rule is that it is essential to the
proper operation of the justice system that cases that have no chance of
success are weeded out at an early stage:
Lameman

at para.
10
. Although
parties are not expected to bring their entire case, they should put their best
foot forward in terms of answering the claim made that it should be dismissed
summarily: at para. 11.

[
42
]

The plaintiffs submit that, among other things, this application is
premature in that the parties have not engaged in examination for discovery. They
submit this is one reason why summary judgment should not be granted:
Xiao v.
Fan
,
2020 BCSC 69
at paras.
48–49
.

[
43
]

They also rely on another principle from
Lameman
that summary
judgment motions are decided on the basis of pleadings and material before the
court, but they ought not to be granted by vague references to what might be
adduced in the future. Thus, there is a balance between holding a party to put
their “best foot” forward, and not dismissing a case too early in the stage of
the litigation.

[
44
]

In this case, both parties filed affidavit evidence. Roman relies on
the affidavits from the Personal Defendants. As I noted, Roman’s position, in
part, is that it could not have breached the non‑compete clause when it
was not a party to the share purchase agreement. It acknowledges the allegation
in the claim that it was aware of a non‑compete clause, but asserts that
there is no evidence to substantiate that allegation.

[
45
]

It also goes further, relying on the affidavit of Jasbir Kochar in
which he says that he is not involved in the Onex store, which was alleged to
be a vehicle through which Roman was selling competing products. He also
deposed that he is not involved at all in the kitchen cabinet hardware or
shower‑door hardware business, which was the subject of the non‑compete
clause.

[
46
]

Similarly, Dilpreet Joura filed an affidavit. He is the owner of
the Onex company. He explained that there used to be two shareholders of
Northam, which were: (1) the other plaintiff, 105, which was owned by a Mr.
Ahuja; and (2) Wipro.  Wipro is a company in which the Personal Defendants are
involved.

[
47
]

Mr. Joura alleges that at one time Mr. Ahuja, while they were
still shareholders in Northam, began disrupting the business by diverting
products to a competitor. Mr. Joura deposed that led to a parting of ways,
which ultimately resulted in Wipro selling its shares in Northam to 105. Mr.
Joura similarly deposed that he has no financial interest in Roman and is not
involved in its business in any way.

[
48
]

The plaintiffs rely on two affidavits from Mr. Ahuja. He is the
director of Northam, and he alleges that Roman was incorporated after the non‑compete
clause was entered into. He explained in his affidavit why he wanted the non‑compete
clause in the share purchase agreement. He alleges that Roman and Onex operate
out of premises that are owned by Onex.

[
49
]

Mr. Ahuja also deposed that he asked a relative to visit the Onex
store as a mystery shopper. He stated that this person bought products that
identified in the restrictive covenant as items for which the Personal Defendants
could not engage in business. He attached receipts and photographs to
substantiate this fact. He also described noticing a decline in sales to
particular customers, who he claimed informed him were getting products from
Roman.

[
50
]

Roman emphasizes that much of evidence is hearsay, and the pleadings
do not contain those allegations. While that is true, on an application for
summary judgment, the court is permitted to look at evidence.

[
51
]

However, Roman submits the more important point is that the
description in Mr. Ahuja’s affidavit of the sale of items alleged to have
constituted a breach cannot be so. It submits there is a fatal flaw to the
plaintiffs’ allegations because there are two different versions in the record of
the share purchase agreement and the non‑compete clause.

[
52
]

Roman submits that the plaintiffs have merely pointed to products listed
in the appendix to the agreement as proof of the breach of the non-compete
clause, alleging that it lists items that sold by Roman through Onex. However,
the specific pages that list those products are not initialled by the parties, unlike
other pages. Both of the Personal Defendants deposed that when they signed the share
purchase agreement, they initialled every page. Roman submits that the pages
not initialled cannot be said to form a part of the agreement and, therefore,
there is no evidence on the summary dismissal application about the potential
breach of the non-compete agreement.

[
53
]

Mr. Ahuja’s affidavit explained why those pages are not
initialled. He deposed that the Personal Defendants’ lawyer requested the
schedule of items be included at the time, after signing. The plaintiffs submit
the Personal Defendants cannot now deny the validity or effectiveness of those
pages.

[
54
]

What this means is that there is a dispute on facts fundamental to the
claim —the content of the non‑compete clause. As noted in
Lameman
,
where there is a dispute that cannot be resolved by looking at the evidence
itself, I am bound to assume the version most favourable to the plaintiffs is true.
That is simply a reflection that summary judgment is not meant to be a forum in
which disputed material facts are decided.

[
55
]

Roman points out that it denies selling any of those products in the
first place. Therefore, it says the allegation that there was a relationship,
or somehow that the two Personal Defendants were involved, is denied in its
affidavit evidence. Its position is that this is a conflict that cannot be
decided on the basis of the evidence before the Court, and that is a fundamental
dispute. Therefore, while Roman is not a party to the non‑compete clause and
can legitimately assert that this issue is separate from the allegations made
against it, the dispute is a fulcrum upon which the conspiracy claim is made.

[
56
]

Roman is not a party to the agreement, but the evidence before me is
disputed as to what constitutes that agreement. Therefore, I am unable to say
that the plaintiffs’ claim is bound to fail because those types of conflicts ought
not to be decided on a summary judgment application.

[
57
]

For all those reasons, I am unable to grant summary judgment in this
case, and I therefore dismiss the application brought under R. 9‑6.

Security for Costs

[
58
]

In the further alternative, Roman sought an
order for security of costs based on
s. 236
of
Business Corporations Act
,
S.B.C. 2002, c. 57. That section allows such an order to be granted where it
appears a corporation is unable to pay costs if the defendant were to be
successful.

[
59
]

Both parties agreed that the applicable test is
set out in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
91 A.C.W.S. (3d) 362,
1999 CanLII 5860 (B.C.S.C.)
:

[14]      … the test to be applied on an
application for security for costs is as follows:

1. Does it appear
that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the defendants’ costs if the
action fails?

2. If so, has the
plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of sufficient value to satisfy an
award of costs?

3. Is the court
satisfied that the defendants have an arguable defence to present?

4. Would an order for costs visit undue
hardship on the plaintiff such that it would prevent the plaintiff’s case from
being heard?

[
60
]

I also note the factors identified in
Kropp
v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252,
1997 CanLII 4037 (C.A.)
:

[17]      … The principles … may be summarized
in this way:

1. The court has a
complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in light of all the
relevant circumstances;

2. The possibility
or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from pursuing its
claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3. The court must
attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an instrument of
oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of
impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4. The court may
have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into detail on
the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5. The court can
order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long as the
amount is more than nominal;

6. Before the
court refuses to order security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle a
valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is
probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7. The lateness of the application for
security is a circumstance which can properly be taken into account.

[
61
]

With regard to the four‑part test, the onus is on the
defendant, although that onus shifts. If the defendant can establish that it
appears the plaintiff would be unable to pay costs, then the onus shifts to the
plaintiff to show that: (i) it has exigible assets of sufficient value; (ii) it
can convince the court that it can still have an arguable defence; and/or (iii)
an order for costs would visit undue hardship on the plaintiff, which would
prevent the plaintiff's case from being heard.

[
62
]

Roman points to its evidence from the personal property register that
the plaintiffs have no exigible assets. Roman also has evidence estimating that
the cost of defending the action is just over $31,000.

[
63
]

The plaintiffs' response is to point to a financial statement that they
filed, which under the column of assets, shows liquid assets of just over $1.18
million, as well as property, plant, and equipment valued at $74,000. They
submit that exceeds the claim that Roman makes. Therefore, the plaintiffs submit
that it cannot be found that they are unable to pay costs on an evidentiary
basis.

[
64
]

When looking at all the evidence, I am unable to conclude that the plaintiffs
are unable to pay the defendants' costs should the defence succeed. Even if
that conclusion was wrong, the plaintiffs have established that they have assets
that could satisfy the estimated costs. Given that finding, I conclude security
for costs should not be ordered. While the defendants clearly have an arguable
defence to the case, that factor is not determinative.

[
65
]

I am not satisfied that an order of security for costs would visit
undue hardship on the plaintiffs. However, as I understand it, the test is
applied sequentially. Since I am not satisfied it has been demonstrated that
the plaintiffs could not satisfy an award, security for costs is not granted.

Production of List of Documents

[
66
]

In the second application, the plaintiffs seek an order that Roman
produce a list of documents within 14 days. They say it is long past the
deadline, and that they made demands in a timely way. I note that the
application is for the production of particular documents, but the plaintiffs
resiled from that position at the hearing.

[
67
]

It is notable that even before or around the time the claim was
amended and before it was added as a party, Roman provided documents that were
identified in the notice of civil claim, namely, the central register and its incorporation
documents.

[
68
]

Roman submits it is virtually impossible for it to know exactly what
it would be responding to, for all the same reasons it raised under the
application to strike or dismiss the claim. It submits that if it is likely
that there is going to be an amendment to provide those particulars, then it
should not be required to produce documents until the claim is clarified.

[
69
]

In addition, Roman points out that the plaintiffs were not just
seeking a list of documents, but production of particular documents, which
obviates the relief being claimed. It submits this point is underscored by the
following: (i) as pleaded, the claim is vague; (ii) its submission that the
pleading was improper; and (iii) there is an inference, or an implication, that
the thrust of the plaintiffs’ application was really to get production of those
particular documents. Roman argues these factors militate against the relief
being sought.

[
70
]

In the overall scheme of things, given that pleadings have closed,
there is no reason why Roman should not produce a list of documents. I do find
its reticence to do so to have a sound basis. While I make no findings to this effect,
I note that the notice of civil claim would improve greatly if particulars were
provided.

[
71
]

As it now stands, it is reasonable for Roman to say it does not know
precisely what documents it is supposed to provide. However, it is not the court's
role to insert itself and force parties to provide those particulars when those
have not been sought, or to order amendments be made to pleadings, even if the court
might view both things as being beneficial. However, in the absence of such relief
being sought, there is no reason why a list of documents cannot be produced. Given
Roman’s position and the comments I have made, the plaintiffs might correctly anticipate
receipt of a thin list of documents, which may be justified given the state of
the pleadings.

[
72
]

While I have not found the lack of clarity identified by Roman to be
sufficient to grant the other remedies sought, it may mean production of
documents will required further litigation by the parties. The plaintiffs suggest
that they were trying to be efficient in anticipating that Roman would not
produce very much, but with respect, that is not how one goes about document
production. It is the plaintiffs' obligation in the first place to make the
pleadings clear.

[
73
]

I point out that it is not alleged that Roman breached the non‑compete
clause, nor could that allegation be made. Therefore, it is difficult to know
what documents the plaintiffs expect to receive. The documents sought probably
focus on the alleged conspiracy that Roman denies based, in part, on its
position that the allegation suffers from vagueness and lack of particularity,
as already discussed.

[
74
]

In particular, I note the failure to identify which particular
defendants are alleged to have engaged in the concerted action. Therefore, it
is understandable why Roman may not have responded to the demand for a list of
documents given its position about these deficiencies. However, that does not
provide a reason why it cannot respond formally to a demand for a list of
documents.

[
75
]

For those reasons, I order that Roman prepare and deliver to the
plaintiffs a list of documents within 21 days of today.

“Sharma J.”
